The host comparison does not lowercase either side, so a mixed-case host is wrongly rejected. This fails closed and is not a bypass. Normalize case on both sides of the comparison (e.g. downcase both) to avoid false rejections.

comentarios.texto: `request.referer` is interpolated unescaped into an inline script string. A referer on the allowed host with a single quote in its path can break out of the string and run script (XSS). Build the target origin from the validated URI (scheme://host[:port]) and output it with `to_json`/`j`.

goldens: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

hist.text: layouts/embed.html.erb:11 writes '<%= request.referer %>' inside a JavaScript string; Rails 3.2.12 (Gemfile.lock) html_escape does not escape single quotes, so a referer on the allowed host whose path contains a quote can break out of the string literal and inject script.

app/views/layouts/embed.html.erb:11 uses ordinary escaped ERB output, not raw or html_safe. Rails escapes apostrophes and angle brackets, so the claimed single-quote breakout does not occur; see the [Rails escaping implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rails/rails/v3.2.12/activesupport/lib/active_support/core_ext/string/output_safety.rb).

Concede. I was wrong about Rails 3.2.12: activesupport-3.2.12 output_safety.rb has `HTML_ESCAPE = { ... '"' => '"', "'" => ''' }` and `s.gsub(/[&"'><]/, HTML_ESCAPE)`. layouts/embed.html.erb:11 `'<%= request.referer %>'` uses escaped output, and entities are not decoded inside <script>, so a quote in the referer cannot close the JS string and `<` cannot close the script. No XSS.

goldens: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

comentarios.texto: Call passes {} as data to updateManyByCredentialId: await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}). WHAT: `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty `data` object, but `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is a Prisma `@updatedAt` field that only updates when the write changes at least one field. WHY: Prisma treats `data: {}` as a no-op (it is accepted syntactically but performs no field change), so the stated intent — 'Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential' — never happens and the calendars' timestamps stay stale. HOW: pass an explicit field, e.g. `updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, { updatedAt: new Date() })` (or set a real business column), so the timestamp is actually refreshed.

The new call does not actually refresh SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. updateManyByCredentialId in the other changed file forwards `data` unchanged to Prisma, and Prisma does not advance an @updatedAt field when the update data is empty. Consequently successful availability refreshes leave the selected-calendar timestamps unchanged despite this call's stated purpose. Pass an explicit timestamp, e.g. `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`, or make the repository method explicitly perform the timestamp update.

`updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId, {})` passes an empty data object, and Prisma may not set `@updatedAt` when no fields are written. The SelectedCalendar.updatedAt timestamp may then never change, so the intended cache-refresh marker is not recorded. Set an explicit field in the data, for example `{ updatedAt: new Date() }`.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.

Search initialization already starts a background consumer at pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:202-213 before initWatcher can fail at server.go:755-757, leaving that consumer and its backend poller running after constructor failure.

Leaving that aside, a constructor failure aborts storage-server startup, so the uncancelled s.ctx has no practical effect. Real but cleanup-level.

The missing lifecycle cleanup has a concrete effect beyond the uncancelled context. Search initialization starts a SQL poller before initWatcher makes another WatchWriteEvents call, whose database query can fail. The constructor then discards the server without calling lifecycle.Stop, which cancels the backend’s pollers (sql/backend.go:119,558-585). Calling s.cancel alone is insufficient, as the reviewer notes, but that does not make the leaked background work a nit.

Agreed lifecycle.Stop is also skipped, so the SQL poller started by search init survives. But every caller propagates the error and aborts startup: sql/server.go:77 `rs, err := resource.NewResourceServer(opts)` -> sql/service.go:113 and unified/client.go:101 return err. Leaked work only exists in a process that is failing to start (server.go:258-261 `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server"...); return nil, err`). Cleanup on a fatal path: nit.

I retain TP: this is a resource-lifecycle bug. Search initialization starts a background consumer and SQL poller before initWatcher performs another fallible database query. The new constructor error path discards the server without stopping that work; the poller requires backend.Stop to cancel b.done. Propagating a startup error does not itself terminate the process or release those resources, although prompt process exit limits the impact.

Agreed on the facts: server.go:258-261 returns nil, err without s.cancel() or lifecycle.Stop, so the search poller survives. You also note that a prompt process exit limits the impact. Every caller propagates the error and aborts startup (sql/server.go:77 -> sql/service.go:113, unified/client.go:101), so the leak only exists in a process that is failing to start. Cleanup on a fatal path: nit.

The new constructor error path discards a partially initialized server without lifecycle cleanup. The cited callers propagate the error but do not stop this background work. Eventual process termination limits the impact, but the surviving database activity makes this a resource-lifecycle defect worth reporting.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator returns success without consuming the accepted code. The external storage retains the entire generated list, and getCredentials reconstructs a fresh model from that same list each time, so logging out and logging in again with the same recovery code succeeds indefinitely. This breaks the single-use recovery-code invariant (and concurrent validations can both accept the same code). Consume the accepted code in external storage atomically with validation, and add a second-login/replay test that requires the used code to be rejected.

WHAT: federated recovery-code validation only checks anyMatch(key equals input) and never consumes/burns the used code. WHY: a single recovery code can be replayed indefinitely for that user, defeating single-use recovery semantics that the local provider enforces by removing the used code. HOW: remove the matched code from the stored list (and persist/return updated credential) on successful validation, mirroring single-use consumption.

hist.text: BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid returns generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key.equals(input)) (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:326-340) without removing the matched code, so a code can be reused. This is a testsuite provider; production consumption is the provider's responsibility.

BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:334-340 checks membership without modifying the stored codes, and getCredentials at lines 237-242 reconstructs them from that unchanged list. Successful validation therefore permits replay and never advances exhaustion, unlike RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.java:109-111.

This is a testsuite fixture, not product code: testsuite/.../testsuite-providers/.../BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.java:340 `return generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()));`. It stores codes as a plain JSON list in an in-memory test user (line 334); consumption in a real federated store is that provider's job. A test double not modelling single-use has no effect on what Keycloak does for users: test tidying, nit.

Changed to TP/nit. The new validator does leave accepted codes reusable, but it belongs exclusively to a testsuite provider that already simplifies authentication, including accepting a hardcoded OTP. The added test verifies federated setup and login, not consumption or exhaustion, and this fixture does not govern production providers’ validation. The evidence establishes an incomplete test double, not a production replay vulnerability or a test failing to verify its stated behavior.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The exclusive lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the blocking file read / synchronous CDN HTTP request (lines 56-67) and there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. WHY: On a cold cache, all concurrent callers (api/index.go:82, api/frontendsettings.go:62, middleware/recovery.go:141) block on the write lock and then each sequentially re-executes the full load (file I/O or blocking http.DefaultClient.Do), producing a thundering-herd serialization and N redundant loads instead of one; in Dev mode this happens on every request since the fast path is skipped, serializing all concurrent page loads. HOW: after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` re-check the cache (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) so only the first goroutine performs the load, and drop the defer in favor of releasing the lock immediately after assigning `entryPointAssetsCache = result` to avoid holding it during I/O.

The cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent production requests that initially observe a nil cache each reload and decode the manifest even after another request has populated it. During a cold-start request burst, these redundant filesystem reads and JSON decodes execute serially under the global lock, delaying queued page and frontend-settings requests and blocking cache readers while each reload runs. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env != setting.Dev before performing asset loading.

The cache is not re-checked after taking the write lock (no double-checked locking). Concurrent callers that saw a nil cache each re-read and re-parse the manifest serially while holding the exclusive lock, which blocks all readers. Fix: after Lock(), re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`.

WHAT: Write path does check-then-lock without re-checking the cache after acquiring the exclusive lock. WHY: A second concurrent cache-miss waits on Lock, then reloads and unconditionally overwrites entryPointAssetsCache (line 69), wiping a valid entry just installed by the first loader — including overwriting it with nil when its own file/CDN load fails — causing spurious errors and redundant loads. HOW: Re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after Lock() and return early, and do not assign cache when result is nil/err != nil.

goldens: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

hist.text: After entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() (webassets.go:48-49) the cache is not re-checked, so concurrent cold-start callers that saw nil each reload the manifest serially. The effect is a few redundant file reads at startup; results are identical.

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:41-49 checks the cache before acquiring the write lock but never rechecks afterward, so concurrent misses can each execute the load at line 60 serially. The newly introduced lock therefore turns redundant loads into blocking work for queued requests and cache readers.

Agreed the re-check is missing (webassets.go:48-49 `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(); defer ...Unlock()` with no cache check after). But the only effect is that a cold-start burst re-reads one small local manifest serially (CDN path is dead: :54 `cdn := ""`), producing identical results, once per process. Before the PR the same loads ran concurrently with a data race. Redundant work with no user effect: nit, low.

Changed to TP/nit: webassets.go:48 lacks a cache recheck, permitting redundant serialized loads by callers that already observed nil. However, cdn := "" disables HTTP fetching, and subsequent production callers return the populated cache; the code establishes minor redundant work rather than a meaningful performance regression. Severity remains medium under the required rubric because the issue as stated claims meaningful request delays and spurious failures, which severity assessment must assume true.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Exclusive entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() is held across blocking file read (readWebAssetsFromFile) and HTTP fetch (readWebAssetsFromCDN). WHY: Serializes all concurrent GetWebAssets callers on disk/network latency and blocks RLock fast-path readers behind the pending writer; in Dev mode where the cache is bypassed every request serializes on file I/O. HOW: Load outside the exclusive lock (double-check, load, then lock only to publish) or use singleflight/sync.Once for the cold-miss path.

hist.text: Holding the write lock while loading (webassets.go:48-69) is the intended way to populate the cache; the CDN path is dead (cdn := ""), and in production the load happens only at cold start. Dev-mode serialization of a small file read is not a defect.

The new exclusive lock at pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48-49 remains held through the file read and decoding at lines 60 and 75-82. Because development mode bypasses the cache return at line 45, concurrent development requests now serialize their manifest loads; the claimed HTTP latency is inapplicable because lines 54-55 disable CDN fetching.

The comment's main cost, the blocking HTTP fetch, is dead code: webassets.go:54-55 `cdn := ""` / `if cdn != "" { result, err = readWebAssetsFromCDN(...) }`. What remains is holding the write lock while reading a local manifest, which in production happens once at cold start; dev-mode serialization of a local file read is not a defect. Populating a cache under its write lock is correct, intended behaviour.

Changed to FP: holding the write lock during cache initialization is valid synchronization, and webassets.go:54 makes the claimed HTTP fetch unreachable. Development requests do serialize local manifest loading, but serialization alone does not establish a meaningful performance defect. The missing production cache recheck is covered separately by issue #01.

comentarios.texto: The new validation-failure warning logs `raw_report`, the full unvalidated report object supplied by the caller. This endpoint is public and unauthenticated (permission_classes = (), @csrf_exempt), so the payload is attacker-controlled, and browser report bodies routinely carry sensitive values (CSP blocked-uri/document-uri/script-sample, sourceFile, plus the full user_agent). Logging the raw payload on every validation failure writes potentially sensitive data into application logs; log only the report `type` (or a sanitized/redacted subset) instead of the entire raw object.

Do not attach the complete raw report to the validation warning. Browser reports contain page URLs (potentially including tokens or personal data in query strings) and arbitrary body contents. Any invalid field now causes that entire payload to be emitted at warning level, exposing it in operational logs even where the existing info-level request logging is filtered out. Log the failed field names/report type or a redacted diagnostic instead.

hist.text: Line 113 logs raw_report on validation failure. The same unauthenticated payload is already logged in full at line 93 (request_body, pre-existing) and line 102, so the new field adds no new exposure; it is a log-context detail.

src/sentry/issues/endpoints/browser_reporting_collector.py:111-113 newly attaches the entire caller-supplied report to a warning without redaction. This exposes URLs and arbitrary body contents at warning level even when the existing info-level logging at line 93 is suppressed.

The same unauthenticated payload is already logged unredacted on every request: browser_reporting_collector.py:93 `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})`, and the pre-existing :102 `extra={..., "data": raw_data}` on invalid format. The new :113 `"raw_report": report` logs a subset of what is already logged; no new data class reaches the logs, only a different level. Log-context detail, not a new exposure.

I retain TP: this is a security defect because the new warning includes the complete unredacted report. The existing info log can be suppressed through the supported log-level configuration while warnings remain enabled. The pre-existing invalid-format warning only handles non-list requests, so it does not cover this validation-failure path.

The 'info can be suppressed' scenario is hypothetical: browser_reporting_collector.py:93 `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})` logs the whole unauthenticated payload on every request, and :101-102 already logs `"data": raw_data` at warning. The new :113 `"raw_report": report` is one element of what :93 already logs. No new data reaches the logs; log-context detail.

I retain TP: the PR newly logs the complete unredacted report on validation failure at WARNING. Suppressing INFO is explicitly supported: src/sentry/runner/initializer.py:272–284 applies SENTRY_LOG_LEVEL to the sentry logger, so WARNING suppresses the existing request-body log while retaining this new disclosure. The pre-existing invalid-format warning handles only non-list requests and cannot run for the list payloads reaching this validation branch. This changes sensitive-data exposure under a supported configuration, rather than merely adding log context.

Conceded. src/sentry/runner/initializer.py:272-284 applies SENTRY_LOG_LEVEL to the overridable loggers, so a supported WARNING setting suppresses `logger.info("browser_report_received", extra={"request_body": request.data})` (browser_reporting_collector.py:93). The pre-existing warning at :100-103 runs only for non-list payloads. Under that config, the new `extra={"validation_errors": serializer.errors, "raw_report": report}` (:111-113) is a new exposure of unauthenticated report contents.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: endpoint loops over unbounded raw_data array validating each report and metrics.incr per report with no size limit. WHY: attacker can POST huge arrays causing CPU/memory blowup and metric spam on unauthenticated endpoint. HOW: enforce max reports per request (e.g. reject >50) before validation.

hist.text: The per-report loop over request.data existed before this PR (base iterated raw_data with metrics.incr per report); the endpoint is gated by an option (line 90) and request size is bounded by Django's upload limit. No new defect introduced.

src/sentry/issues/endpoints/browser_reporting_collector.py:107-127 performs serializer validation for every report and now retains all validated payloads before processing, without a batch limit. I change to FP: the base already processed an uncapped report array and emitted one metric per report. The disabled Django upload limit is also pre-existing. Serializer validation and buffering are new, but my earlier answer did not establish a meaningful performance regression beyond the already-existing unbounded processing described by this issue.

comentarios.texto: The 'preprod_artifact.api.assemble' analytics event is recorded before the feature-flag check at line 88 (and before any validation). When the organization lacks 'organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble' the endpoint returns 404 without assembling anything, but the assemble event has already been emitted, so this metric/analytics event over-counts requests that never performed the operation. Move the analytics.record call to after the feature check (once assembly is actually attempted/succeeds) so the event reflects the operation it names.

WHAT: analytics.record runs before the preprod-artifact-assemble feature check, logging assemble attempts even when disabled/unauthorized. WHY: inflates analytics, leaks usage signal, and does work before guard. HOW: move analytics.record after the feature check (or after validation).

goldens: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

hist.text: organization_preprod_artifact_assemble.py:81-86 adds analytics.record('preprod_artifact.api.assemble') before the features.has check at :88, which returns 404 when the flag is off, so the event is emitted for requests that never assemble anything.

src/sentry/preprod/api/endpoints/organization_preprod_artifact_assemble.py:81-91 records an API invocation before checking availability, but src/sentry/preprod/analytics.py:4-10 defines no successful-assembly contract. The endpoint also handles status polling at lines 111-120, so interpreting this event as a count of completed assemblies is unsupported.

organization_preprod_artifact_assemble.py:81-86 (new) `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before :88 `if not features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` which returns 404. The event is named after the assemble operation, so every request from orgs without the feature is counted as usage of a feature they cannot use; the golden reports exactly this. Misleading product analytics introduced by this PR.

I retain FP: the event records entry into the assemble API, and neither its definition nor any cited consumer establishes that it counts successful or feature-enabled assemblies. This endpoint also handles polling and missing-chunk responses without assembling anything. Recording before the feature check is real, but the event name alone does not establish misleading analytics or a defect.

Concede. organization_preprod_artifact_assemble.py:81-86 records the event on entry, and the same event already fires for status polls and missing-chunk responses (:104-120) that assemble nothing, so it counts API calls, not assemblies. A 404'd call is still an API call; analytics.py:5 defines no stronger contract. Recording before the feature check is intended entry-tracking, not a defect.

comentarios.texto: The retry loop ignores downsize's false return value and retries failed conversions while the file remains oversized. convert_with returns false on converter failure, so an unsupported or malformed oversized image launches the same failing external conversion up to five times per upload without any changed input. Break on a failed downsize result and return an upload error rather than repeating the conversion.

WHAT: Downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value and retries up to 5 times unconditionally while checking tempfile.size. WHY: Failed converts (e.g. SVG, invalid 80%> geometry, corrupt image) burn 5 ImageMagick runs then Upload.create_for still runs with oversized/unmodified file and fails validation, wasting CPU and breaking the feature. HOW: Break on false return and handle failure.

hist.text: The loop at uploads_controller.rb:66-69 ignores OptimizedImage.downsize's return (convert_with returns false on failure), so a failing conversion is repeated up to 5 times; the upload then fails size validation as it would anyway. Only wasted work.

app/models/optimized_image.rb:162 returns false on conversion failure, but app/controllers/uploads_controller.rb:67 ignores that result. An unchanged oversized input therefore triggers up to five identical external conversions before validation, unnecessarily multiplying potentially expensive failed processing.

The loop is bounded (`attempt = 5` ... `attempt -= 1`, uploads_controller.rb:65-68) and a failed conversion leaves the file oversized, so `Upload.create_for` (:72) rejects it exactly as without the retries. It runs inside `Scheduler::Defer.later` (:19-22), not on the request path. The only effect of ignoring `convert_with`'s false (optimized_image.rb:162) is up to four repeated failing convert runs on a bad upload: redundant work, nit.

I retain TP: the new loop ignores conversion failure and can execute the same failing external conversion five times. This can multiply expensive image processing without making progress, delaying upload completion and other deferred work. Under Unicorn, deferred work also occupies the request-serving worker, so unchanged validation results do not make the repeated processing a nit.

I accept that deferred work occupies the Unicorn worker (99-unicorn.rb, defer.rb process_client -> Defer.do_all_work). But this issue is only about ignoring `convert_with`'s false. That changes nothing on the success path: a successful downsize shrinks the file, and the `while ... tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` condition (uploads_controller.rb:66) ends the loop. On the failure path the upload is rejected by `Upload.create_for` (:72), the same outcome as with a break. The only cost is up to four extra failing `convert` runs on a corrupt or unsupported image: redundant work with no user-visible effect, so nit. The worker-occupancy cost of the loop as a whole is issue #08.

I retain TP: the new loop ignores conversion failure and can repeat the same failed external conversion four additional times. Synchronous API uploads call create_upload directly (uploads_controller.rb:15–17), and asynchronous uploads publish their result only after it finishes (:19–21). These retries delay completion and occupy the Unicorn worker; expensive conversion failures therefore have a meaningful performance effect despite unchanged validation results. This finding concerns avoidable retries after failure, independently of the cost of successful downsizing.

Keep nit. The scope is only ignoring `convert_with`'s false return (optimized_image.rb:162). On success the loop condition `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` (uploads_controller.rb:66) ends it, so the success path is unaffected. On failure the upload is rejected by `Upload.create_for` (:72) with or without a break. The only difference is up to four extra failing convert runs on a corrupt or unsupported oversized image, an edge case for an upload that fails anyway. Redundant work with no change in outcome: nit. The cost of the loop as a whole belongs to the other issue (#08).

The newly added loop ignores downsize’s false result and can repeat an unchanged, failing external conversion four additional times. These subprocess calls block completion: synchronous uploads await create_upload, asynchronous uploads publish afterward, and Unicorn drains deferred work before serving another request. Expensive conversion failures therefore multiply upload latency and worker occupancy even though validation ultimately rejects the file. This is a meaningful performance defect specifically in failure handling, independent of the cost of successful downsizing.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Up to 5 synchronous OptimizedImage.downsize + ImageOptim convert runs execute inline in create_upload request cycle for every oversized image. WHY: Blocks the Rails request thread with CPU-intensive shell-outs per upload, enabling easy request-thread exhaustion/DoS with large images. HOW: Move downsizing to background job or enforce single-pass/timeout.

hist.text: The inline downsize loop (uploads_controller.rb:64-70) is bounded to 5 attempts on files capped at 10 MB, and this controller already processes uploads synchronously; moving it to a background job is a design preference, not a defect.

app/controllers/uploads_controller.rb:65-68 adds up to five synchronous conversion-and-optimization passes, implemented at app/models/optimized_image.rb:160-164. Although ordinary uploads use Scheduler::Defer, config/initializers/99-unicorn.rb:5 installs the hook at lib/scheduler/defer.rb:83-87 that drains deferred work on the Unicorn worker after responding, so expensive uploads still occupy request-serving workers.

The claim that this blocks the request thread is wrong for normal uploads: `Scheduler::Defer.later("Create Upload") do data = create_upload(...)` (uploads_controller.rb:19-21) and the response is rendered right after (:23); only API `synchronous` calls run inline (:15-16). The work is bounded to 5 passes over a file already capped (FileHelper.download 10.megabytes, :55), alongside the existing synchronous thumbnail/orientation work in Upload.create_for. Moving it to a job is a design preference, not a defect.

I retain TP: config/initializers/99-unicorn.rb installs Scheduler::Defer::Unicorn, whose process_client drains deferred work before returning the worker to request handling. Rendering the response first therefore does not free that worker during the new conversion loop. The five-pass bound does not bound processing cost, and the cited 10 MB limit applies only to URL downloads. Existing image processing does not eliminate the additional worker occupancy introduced by these passes.

Conceded. My two facts were wrong. The deferred block does tie up the request-serving worker: 99-unicorn.rb extends the server with Scheduler::Defer::Unicorn, whose `process_client` runs `super(client); Defer.do_all_work` (defer.rb:83-87). And the 10 MB cap applies only to API URL downloads (uploads_controller.rb:55), so it does not bound a direct upload. The PR adds up to five ImageMagick passes (:65-68) on files that were previously rejected cheaply, and that work runs on the Unicorn worker. A real performance defect introduced here.

goldens: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

hist.text: The loop at uploads_controller.rb:65-69 is bounded by attempt = 5 decremented each iteration, so it cannot loop forever; Tempfile#size is not cached but re-read from the file each call.

app/controllers/uploads_controller.rb:65-68 guarantees termination after five attempts, but the stale-size/file-handling concern is real. app/models/optimized_image.rb:164 invokes ImageOptim, whose pinned version [replaces files by renaming](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/toy/image_optim/v0.20.2/lib/image_optim/image_path.rb), leaving the open tempfile handle attached to the previous inode. Consequently, the size checks at line 66 and filesize passed at line 72 can describe the old file, causing unnecessary resizing or incorrect rejection.

Concede TP none. Infinite loop is impossible (attempt counter, uploads_controller.rb:65-68), but the stale-size fact holds: `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!(to)` (optimized_image.rb:164) in image_optim 0.20.2 replaces via `temp.rename(src.to_s)`, so the open Tempfile fd keeps the old inode and `tempfile.size` (:66, :72) reports the old file. The loop check and the filesize passed to Upload.create_for can therefore be wrong. Severity as stated: high.

WHY: concrete `sync_assignee_outbound` overrides without `**kwargs` will raise TypeError on the new kwarg, and the status method gains a dead param that is never checked. comentarios.texto: Offsets are only tracked for messages that were submitted, and there is no partition revoke handling. Contiguity is checked with `range(start, max_offset+1)`, so any offset gap (compacted topics, transactional markers, or offsets filtered out upstream) permanently blocks commits for that partition. The `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` state is never cleared on rebalance, so stale state survives partition reassignment. Treat gaps as committable once all lower tracked offsets are complete, and clear per-partition state when partitions are revoked.

Determine the commit boundary from received offsets rather than requiring every integer in this range to exist. Kafka offsets need not be consecutive: if 100, 102 and 103 are delivered and completed, this scan stops at the nonexistent 101 even though there is no unfinished record. Conversely, after committing 100 and removing it, the next scan starts at 102 and commits past the gap, contradicting the added gap tests. Iterate received offsets in sorted order and stop at the first outstanding record; add a test covering legitimate skipped Kafka offsets across multiple commit cycles.

hist.text: queue_consumer.py:86-105: the scan stops at a missing offset only until the lower offset is committed; mark_committed (line 105) drops offsets <= committed, so the next cycle starts at max(last_committed+1, min_offset)=next received offset and commits past the gap. Gaps delay the commit by one cycle, they never block it permanently.

queue_consumer.py:86-93 stops at missing integer offsets, unnecessarily limiting progress to one contiguous run per commit cycle, and result_consumer.py:254-258 reuses the tracker without resetting assignment state. The permanent-stall claim is overstated: queue_consumer.py:105 removes committed entries, allowing the next scan to skip the gap.

You agree the permanent-stall claim is false (queue_consumer.py:105 `self.all_offsets[partition] = {o for o in ... if o > offset}` then :86 `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` jumps the gap next cycle). What remains is a gap costing one extra 1s commit cycle (:276 `wait(1.0)`), which is no defect. On rebalance state: stale last_committed/outstanding are harmless because reassigned partitions resume at our committed offset+1 (result_consumer.py:251) and re-added offsets go through add/complete again. The issue's core fact (gaps block commits permanently) is false -> hallucination.

Keep TP (category: perf), although the permanent-stall claim is incorrect. queue_consumer.py:86-105 advances only one contiguous run per commit cycle, and :276 imposes a one-second wait between cycles. Completed offsets 100, 102, 104, 106 therefore require four cycles, not merely one additional cycle overall. With sustained gaps arriving faster than this, commit lag and retained offset state grow without bound, making this a meaningful performance defect.

Conceded TP, though on the rebalance claim rather than the gap or performance one. The gap part is mostly moot: filtered and errored messages are tracked (queue_consumer.py:301-304, :319-325), so only Kafka-level gaps occur. The comment's other claim does hold. The factory reuses one queue_pool and its OffsetTracker across assignments (result_consumer.py:254-258 `queue_pool=self.queue_pool`), and nothing resets `last_committed`/`all_offsets` on revoke (queue_consumer.py:44-46, :100-105). If completed offsets from before a revoke are still uncommitted when the partition returns, the scan starting at `max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` (:86) commits those stale offsets, which can rewind the group's committed offset. Severity high as stated.
